## Warm-up · three questions from last time

[<span class="pause-cue">≈ 5 min</span> · shout it out]{.eyebrow}

::: {.card}
1. Which weight matrices does an RNN reuse at every time step?
2. Why do gradients vanish over long sequences in a vanilla RNN?
3. A vanilla RNN has $h_t = \tanh(0.5\,h_{t-1} + 1.0\,x_t)$, with $h_0 = 0$ and $x_1 = 1$. What is $h_1$?
:::

## Warm-up · answers

::: {.card}
1. **All of them.** $\mathbf{W}_{hh}$, $\mathbf{W}_{xh}$ and $\mathbf{b}_h$ are the same at every time step. That reuse *is* the parameter sharing — one model, applied $T$ times.
2. **Backprop through time multiplies one step-to-step factor per step** ($W_{hh}$ times a $\tanh'$ term). When those factors sit below 1, the product shrinks towards 0: $0.9^{50} \approx 0.005$.
3. $h_1 = \tanh(0.5 \times 0 + 1.0 \times 1) = \tanh(1) \approx 0.76$.
:::

# Part 1 · The attention operation in three layers {background-color="#0E1A2B"}

## Layer 1 of 3 — the intuition

[Reading a sentence]{.eyebrow}

> *The keys, which had been sitting on the table next to the mail, **were** still there.*

To choose the verb form *were* (not *was*), the model has to look back **~12 tokens** — a dozen positions — to find *keys* and ignore *table* and *mail*.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[An RNN]{.pill-amber}

"Hopes" the relevant info survives a dozen hidden-state updates.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Attention]{.pill-green}

At the position of *were*, **look at every previous token directly** and decide which to focus on.
:::
:::

::: {.card}
"Attention" — the network gets to look anywhere it wants, and learns where to look.
:::

## What does attention do?

::: {.card}
**For each position, take a weighted average of the representations at other positions — where the weights are computed from the data itself.**

* "Weighted average": linear combination.
* "Of representations": each token's vector.
* "Weights computed from the data": the model **learns** which other positions to look at, given the current one.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Notice this is a **soft** version of "select one token". Instead of picking one, attention takes a **weighted blend** of all of them, with weights summing to 1.
:::

## Attention as a soft database lookup

[A useful analogy]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Imagine a database:

* Each row has a **key** and a **value**.
* You issue a **query**.
* The database returns values whose keys match.

Attention is the **soft** version:

* Every key gets a *similarity score* with the query.
* Return a *weighted average* of all values.
* Weights come from softmax of the similarity scores.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.card}
**Why "soft"?** Because the weights are continuous and differentiable. We can backprop through them.

  * A hard database lookup is non-differentiable.

Attention smooths the lookup, enabling the model to *learn* what to attend to.
:::
:::
:::

## Layer 2 of 3 — queries, keys, values

For each token position $i$, produce **three** vectors from its embedding $\mathbf{x}_i$ via learned matrices $\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V$:

$$
\mathbf{q}_i = \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{W}_Q, \quad \mathbf{k}_i = \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{W}_K, \quad \mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{W}_V
$$

::: {.card}
[Mental model]{.eyebrow}

* **Query** $\mathbf{q}_i$ — *"what am I looking for?"*
* **Key** $\mathbf{k}_j$ — *"what do I offer?"*
* **Value** $\mathbf{v}_j$ — *"if you attend to me, here's the content I'll contribute."*

The three are projections of the *same* embedding through *different* learned matrices.

  * A token offers different "search terms" than it offers as "search results".
  
:::

## The attention score — how much should $i$ attend to $j$?

Take the **dot product** of $\mathbf{q}_i$ and $\mathbf{k}_j$.

* Large positive ⇒ $\mathbf{q}_i$ and $\mathbf{k}_j$ point the same way ⇒ $i$ should attend strongly to $j$.
* Around zero ⇒ no relationship.
* Large negative ⇒ they point opposite ⇒ $i$ should *not* attend to $j$.

::: {.card}
Stack the queries and keys as matrices $\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$ (one row per token, $T$ tokens, $d$ dimensions each):

$$
\text{scores} = \frac{\mathbf{Q} \mathbf{K}^\mathsf{T}}{\sqrt{d}}, \qquad \text{shape: } (T \times T)
$$

Each entry $(i, j)$ = how much $i$ wants to attend to $j$.

The $\sqrt{d}$ scaling keeps dot products from blowing up in high dimensions.

[Strictly, the scale is $\sqrt{d_k}$, the **key dimension** — here a single head uses the full width $d$, so $d_k = d$. Once we split into $h$ heads (next part), each head works in $d_k = d/h$ and scales by $\sqrt{d/h}$ — exactly what the code does.]{.muted}
:::

## Why divide by $\sqrt{d}$? — the problem

Worked example of the blow-up:

::: {.card}
Suppose each entry of $\mathbf{q}_i$ and $\mathbf{k}_j$ has mean 0 and variance 1. The dot product adds up $d$ products, one per dimension:

$$
\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j = q_{i1} k_{j1} + q_{i2} k_{j2} + \cdots + q_{id} k_{jd}
$$

Each term has variance 1. Summing $d$ independent terms gives variance $d$.
:::

::: {.card}
At $d = 64$: variance 64, so standard deviation $\sqrt{64} = 8$.

Raw scores land around $\pm 8$.
:::

This then feeds into the softmax...

## Why divide by $\sqrt{d}$? — what big scores do

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Scores $[2, 0, -2]$]{.pill-green}

$$
\text{softmax} = [0.87, \ 0.12, \ 0.02]
$$

One position leads. The others keep some weight — the output is still a blend, and every position gets a gradient.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Same scores × 4: $[8, 0, -8]$]{.pill-amber}

$$
\text{softmax} = [0.9997, \ 0.0003, \ 0.0000]
$$

One position takes everything. The gradients through the near-zero entries die, so the model cannot learn to look elsewhere.
:::
:::

::: {.card}
Dividing the scores by $\sqrt{d}$ puts them back at variance 1 — the left-hand column, not the right. The softmax stays spread out, and attention stays trainable.
:::


## Softmax → weights → weighted sum

Take softmax across each row of `scores` — gives a probability distribution over positions:

$$
\mathbf{A} = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\mathsf{T}}{\sqrt{d}}\right), \quad \sum_j A_{ij} = 1
$$

::: {.card}
[Worked softmax — one row of scores $[1, 0, 1]$]{.eyebrow}

$$
e^{1} = 2.72, \quad e^{0} = 1, \quad e^{1} = 2.72, \qquad \text{sum} = 6.44
$$

$$
\left[\tfrac{2.72}{6.44}, \ \tfrac{1}{6.44}, \ \tfrac{2.72}{6.44}\right] = [0.42, \ 0.16, \ 0.42]
$$

The two equal-and-largest scores share most of the weight; the small one keeps a little. The weights sum to 1.
:::

Now use the weights to mix the **values**:

$$
\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{V}
$$

::: {.card}
For each position $i$, the output is a **weighted sum** of all value vectors $\mathbf{v}_j$, with weights $A_{ij}$ chosen by the model.

That's the whole attention operation: three matmuls and a softmax.
:::

## Self-attention vs cross-attention

[Same operation, two different uses]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Self-attention]{.pill-blue}

Q, K, V all come from the **same** sequence.

* Used in GPT, Claude, BERT.
* Each token attends to other tokens in the same input.
* This is what we've described so far.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Cross-attention]{.pill}

Q comes from one sequence; K, V come from **another**.

* Used in translation (decoder attends to encoder).
* Used in text-to-image diffusion (image attends to text prompt).
* Used in Whisper (decoder attends to audio).
:::
:::

::: {.card}
**One operation, two roles**: looking within your*self* or looking a*cross* a paired sequence.

* The arithmetic remains the same, it just changes *where you draw Q, K, V from*.

:::

## Layer 3 of 3 — causal masking

For language *generation*, position $t$ must not see positions $t+1, t+2, \ldots$ — that would be cheating/seeing the future.

:::

[Row = the token doing the looking; column = the token it may look at. $1 + 2 + \cdots + 6 = 21$ of the $36$ pairs survive.]{.smaller .muted}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.card}
**Causal mask**: before the softmax, set all entries where $j > i$ to $-\infty$. After softmax, those entries become zero.

The attention matrix becomes **lower-triangular**. Each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.callout-tip}
# Next-token prediction
Causal masking turns "see the whole sentence" attention (used in BERT) into "next-token prediction" attention (used in GPT).
:::
:::
:::

## Attention end to end — the projections

[Three tokens, four dimensions, one head. One click per step.]{.eyebrow}

We have every piece now. Let's run the whole operation by hand on `the cat sat` — three tokens, a 4-number embedding each.

:::

:::

**Step 1** · three tokens, each a 4-number embedding — the rows of $\mathbf{X}$.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Step 2** · every row is multiplied by the same $4 \times 4$ matrix $\mathbf{W}_Q$.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**Step 3** · $\mathbf{q}_{sat} = \mathbf{x}_{sat}\mathbf{W}_Q$, one dot product per column: $(1,1,1,0)\cdot(0,0,1,0) = 1$, $(1,1,1,0)\cdot(1,1,0,0) = 2$, $(1,1,1,0)\cdot(0,0,0,1) = 0$, $(1,1,1,0)\cdot(1,0,0,0) = 1$.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
**Step 4** · every token now has a query. The same three embeddings, through $\mathbf{W}_K$ and $\mathbf{W}_V$, give $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{V}$.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.card}
[The other two projections, done the same way]{.eyebrow}

$$
\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
\mathbf{V} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

One row per token, in order: *the*, *cat*, *sat*.

[Real weight matrices hold floats. Small integers here so you can check every step.]{.smaller .muted}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.card}
In this toy example, every value vector ends in a **1**. Since attention weights sum to 1, whatever the model chooses to look at, that last column will have to come out as 1.
:::
:::
:::

## Attention end to end — the scores

[Every query meets every key: nine dot products, one 3 × 3 matrix]{.eyebrow}

::: {.r-stack}

COLOR="#C58A12">&#8722;&#8734;</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#C58A12"><FONT COLOR="#C58A12">&#8722;&#8734;</FONT></TD></TR><TR><TD BORDER="0"><FONT COLOR="#5C6473">cat</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">0</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">1</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#C58A12"><FONT COLOR="#C58A12">&#8722;&#8734;</FONT></TD></TR><TR><TD BORDER="0"><FONT COLOR="#5C6473">sat</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">1</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">2</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">1</FONT></TD></TR></TABLE></TD></TR></TABLE></TD></TR></TABLE>>];
}
```
:::

:::

**Step 1** · one entry, written out: $\mathbf{q}_{sat} \cdot \mathbf{k}_{cat} = 1 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 + 0 \times 1 + 1 \times 0 = 4$.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Step 2** · divide every entry by $\sqrt{d} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**Step 3** · the mask: *cat* may not look at *sat*. Everything above the diagonal becomes $-\infty$.
:::

::: {.card}
The mask goes on **after** the scores are computed, not before — we work out all nine numbers and then throw three away. This is the `masked_fill` line you'll see in the lab, and it is why the cost stays $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ even though close to half the matrix is discarded.
:::

## Attention end to end — softmax and the output

[The last two steps]{.eyebrow}

::: {.r-stack}

4)</FONT></TD></TR></TABLE></TD></TR><TR><TD><TABLE BORDER="0" CELLBORDER="1" CELLSPACING="0" CELLPADDING="5"><TR><TD BORDER="0"><FONT COLOR="#5C6473">the</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">2.00</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">0.00</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">0.00</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#1A6FB4"><FONT COLOR="#1A6FB4">1.00</FONT></TD></TR><TR><TD BORDER="0"><FONT COLOR="#5C6473">cat</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">0.54</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">2.92</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">0.00</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#1A6FB4"><FONT COLOR="#1A6FB4">1.00</FONT></TD></TR><TR><TD BORDER="0"><FONT COLOR="#5C6473">sat</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">0.42</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">2.32</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#D7D2C5"><FONT COLOR="#0E1A2B">0.42</FONT></TD><TD COLOR="#1A6FB4"><FONT COLOR="#1A6FB4">1.00</FONT></TD></TR></TABLE></TD></TR></TABLE></TD></TR></TABLE>>];
}
```
:::

:::

**Step 1** · softmax the *sat* row: $e^1 = 2.72$, $e^2 = 7.39$, $e^1 = 2.72$, summing to $12.83$ — so the weights are $[0.21,\ 0.58,\ 0.21]$.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Step 2** · mix the values with those weights: $0.21(2,0,0,1) + 0.58(0,4,0,1) + 0.21(0,0,2,1)$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**Step 3** · $= (0.42,\ 2.32,\ 0.42,\ 1.00)$. Row 1 could only look at itself, so its output is $\mathbf{v}_{the}$ exactly.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
**Step 4** · the last column comes out 1 in every row — since *here* the weights sum to 1
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
Read the bottom row. *sat*'s output is **58% cat**, 21% *the*, 21% itself. The verb has pulled in its subject, and that blend is now the vector representing *sat* for the rest of the network.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
Every number came out of three matrix multiplications and one softmax. The only things learned are $\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V$ — $3 \times 16 = 48$ weights in this toy, biases aside.
:::
:::
:::

## Stop and take stock

[<span class="pause-cue">Stop & check</span>]{.eyebrow}

::: {.try-box}
[Try — 90 seconds]{.try-label}

We have $T = 4$ tokens in our sequence. Embedding dimension $d = 8$.

**Question**: what's the shape of the attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$? And what's the shape of the output of $\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V})$?
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.reveal-box}
[Answer]{.reveal-label}
$\mathbf{A}$: shape $(T \times T) = (4 \times 4)$.

Attention output: $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{V}$, shape $(T \times d) = (4 \times 8)$ — same shape as the original token embeddings.

**Attention is shape-preserving.** That's important — it means we can stack attention layers without changing the shape.
:::
:::

# Plenary · attention by hand {background-color="#0E1A2B"}

## Plenary · attention by hand

[<span class="pause-cue">≈ 10 min</span>]{.eyebrow}

::: {.card}
A tiny attention example with $T = 3$ tokens and $d = 2$.

$$
\mathbf{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{V} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 \\ 5 & 5 \end{bmatrix}
$$

($\mathbf{Q}$ and $\mathbf{K}$ happen to be equal here, which keeps the arithmetic short. Self-attention means Q, K and V are drawn from the same sequence — not that the matrices match.)

[Compute, step by step]{.eyebrow}

1. The raw score matrix $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\mathsf{T}$ (no $\sqrt{d}$ scaling and no mask this time — we want the arithmetic bare).
2. Apply softmax row-wise (approximate; "the row's biggest entry gets most of the mass").
3. The attention output $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}$.
4. **Reflect**: what does token 3 (the row $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$) attend to most?
:::

[Six minutes.]{.muted}

## Plenary · answers (1/2)

::: {.card}
[Step 1 — scores]{.eyebrow}

$$
\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\mathsf{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
$$
:::

::: {.card}
[Step 2 — approximate row-softmax]{.eyebrow}

Row 1: $[1, 0, 1] \to \approx [0.42, 0.16, 0.42]$.

Row 2: $[0, 1, 1] \to \approx [0.16, 0.42, 0.42]$.

Row 3: $[1, 1, 2] \to \approx [0.21, 0.21, 0.58]$ (the "2" dominates).
:::

## Plenary · answers (2/2)

::: {.card}
[Step 3 — attention output $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{V}$]{.eyebrow}

Row 3 example:
$$
[0.21, 0.21, 0.58] \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 \\ 5 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = [0.21 \cdot 10 + 0.58 \cdot 5, \ 0.21 \cdot 10 + 0.58 \cdot 5] \approx [5.0, 5.0]
$$
:::

::: {.reveal-box}
[Reflection]{.reveal-label}
Token 3's row is $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ — equal in both dimensions. It scores highest with token 3 itself, which has key $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

So **token 3 attends most strongly to itself**. Tokens with directional keys (like $[1, 0]$ or $[0, 1]$) attend most to *matching* directions.

This is the structure attention learns: tokens with similar Q and K vectors find each other.
:::

# Part 2 · The transformer block {background-color="#0E1A2B"}

## Isn't one head enough?

Our worked example gave *sat* one set of weights: 21% *the*, 58% *cat*, 21% itself. They sum to 1, so they **compete**. Back to the sentence we opened with:

> *The **keys**, which had been sitting on the table next to the mail, **were** still there.*

At the position of *were*, the model needs *keys* — a dozen tokens back — to get the verb form right. 

It also needs the words either side of it to tell that the relative clause has ended

* One distribution has to accommodate for both issues

::: {.card}
**Multi-head attention** [@vaswani2017attention]: run $h$ attention operations side by side, each with its own $\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V$. Each head gets its own weights and its own blend. Concatenate the results, then project once more:

$$
\text{MHA}(\mathbf{X}) = \text{concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, \mathbf{W}_O
$$

Typical $h$: 8, 12, 16, 32. GPT-2 small uses 12.
:::

## Splitting the width into heads

Each head does not get its own full-width copy of the model. The width $d$ is **divided** between them.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
[GPT-2 small, head by head]{.pill-blue}

* $d = 768$, $h = 12$.
* Each head works in $d / h = 64$ dimensions.
* Per head, $\mathbf{W}_Q, \mathbf{W}_K, \mathbf{W}_V$ are each $768 \times 64$.
* Each head still builds a full $T \times T$ score matrix — every token still sees every earlier token.
* Each head scales by $\sqrt{64} = 8$, not $\sqrt{768}$.
* Concatenate 12 outputs of width 64 → 768 again. Then $\mathbf{W}_O$, $768 \times 768$.
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.card}
[Heads are "free"]{.eyebrow}

Twelve heads: $12 \times 3 \times (768 \times 64) = 1{,}769{,}472$ weights.

One full-width head: $3 \times (768 \times 768) = 1{,}769{,}472$.

The heads slice the same budget rather than adding to it. In code it is one $768 \to 2{,}304$ projection followed by a reshape — the QKV line from the parameter slide, which also carried 2,304 biases.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.try-box}
[Try]{.try-label}
GPT-2 large has $d = 1{,}280$ and $h = 20$. How wide is each head, and what does it divide its scores by?
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.reveal-box}
[Answer]{.reveal-label}
$1{,}280 / 20 = 64$ dimensions per head — the same 64 as GPT-2 small — so it divides by $\sqrt{64} = 8$.

Head width sits between 64 and 128 across model generations. What grows is the number of heads.
:::
:::

## Two heads on one sentence

Same three tokens, now with $h = 2$ heads of width 2. Each head has its own $4 \times 2$ projection matrices, so each ends up with its own weights.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Head 1 — the verb finds its subject]{.pill-blue}

$$
\mathbf{A}^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.27 & 0.73 & 0 \\ 0.21 & 0.58 & 0.21 \end{bmatrix}, \;\;
\mathbf{V}^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

*sat* out: $0.21(2,0) + 0.58(0,4) + 0.21(0,2) = (0.42,\ 2.74)$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Head 2 — every token checks the determiner]{.pill-green}

$$
\mathbf{A}^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.73 & 0.27 & 0 \\ 0.58 & 0.21 & 0.21 \end{bmatrix}, \;\;
\mathbf{V}^{(2)} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

*sat* out: $0.58(4,0) + 0.21(0,2) + 0.21(2,0) = (2.74,\ 0.42)$
:::
:::

::: {.card}
Concatenate the two halves: $(0.42,\ 2.74,\ 2.74,\ 0.42)$ — width 4, the shape we started with. $\mathbf{W}_O$ then mixes them, so the next layer sees one vector rather than two stapled together.

One head could not have produced both blends

  * Its row sums to 1 so it has to choose in a way two heads don't!
  
:::

## What do the heads actually learn?

::: {.card}
[Clark et al. (2019) went through every head in BERT and asked what each one attends to]{.eyebrow}

* **Layer 8, head 11**: a determiner attends to the noun it modifies — **94.3%** of the time.
* **Layer 8, head 10**: a direct object attends to its verb — **86.8%**.
* **Layer 5, head 4**: a pronoun attends to the thing it refers to — **65.1%**, against 27% for "just pick the nearest mention" [@clark2019what].

Notice, *again*, these are learned behaviours that emerge from the training objective — for BERT, filling in masked words.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
# No single head captures syntax as a whole
The best head recovers 34.5% of dependency edges, against 26.3% for the rule "attach every word to its right-hand neighbour". Heads specialise on *particular* relations, not on grammar per se.

And most of them are not doing much. Voita et al. (2019) pruned **38 of the 48** encoder heads in a translation model and lost very little performance [@voita2019analyzing].
:::

## The attention formula in code

[Five lines of PyTorch]{.eyebrow}

```python
def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    # Q, K, V are (batch, n_heads, seq_len, d_head)
    scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1)         # (B, h, T, T)
    scores = scores / math.sqrt(Q.size(-1))  # scale by √d
    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -1e9)
    weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)      # (B, h, T, T)
    return weights @ V                       # (B, h, T, d_head)
```

::: {.card}
**Every major transformer — GPT, Claude, BERT —** runs some version of these five lines. The rest is plumbing — splitting heads, applying the mask, projecting the output. The core computation is what you see here.
:::

## One transformer block

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.card}
**Each transformer block is:** LayerNorm → attention → residual; then LayerNorm → MLP → residual.

Repeat this block $N$ times. **That's a transformer.**
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-height: 5.0
digraph G {
  rankdir="TB"; bgcolor="transparent"; ranksep=0.32;
  // Graphviz sizes boxes with fallback metrics for Inter, which the browser
  // renders wider — the extra node margin keeps labels inside their shapes.
  node [fontname="Inter" fontsize=14 margin="0.30,0.14"];
  edge [fontname="Inter" fontsize=13];
  in [shape=box label="input tokens (B × T × d)" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  ln1 [shape=box label="LayerNorm" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  mha [shape=box label="Multi-head attention\n(causal mask)" style=filled fillcolor="#C9322B" fontcolor="white"];
  add1 [shape=circle label="+" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  ln2 [shape=box label="LayerNorm" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  mlp [shape=box label="MLP\n(d → 4d → d)" style=filled fillcolor="#1A6FB4" fontcolor="white"];
  add2 [shape=circle label="+" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  out [shape=box label="output (B × T × d)" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];

  in -> ln1 -> mha -> add1 -> ln2 -> mlp -> add2 -> out;
  in -> add1 [label="  residual" style=dashed];
  add1 -> add2 [label="  residual" style=dashed];
}
```
:::
:::

## Residual connections — why they matter

[The dashed lines in the diagram]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Each sublayer's output is **added** to its input:

$$\mathbf{x}_{\text{out}} = \mathbf{x}_{\text{in}} + f(\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}})$$

* Sublayer learns a **correction** to the input, not the full transformation.
* Differentiating $\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}} + f(\mathbf{x}_{\text{in}})$ gives a **+1** term from the identity path, so the upstream gradient can always flow straight back along that path — it never fully vanishes.
* Stacks of ResNet-style residuals are **the most reliable way** to train networks deeper than ~10 layers.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
First introduced for image CNNs (He et al. 2015 — ResNet). Transformers inherited them. Without residuals, a 100-layer transformer would not train.
:::
:::
:::

## LayerNorm — the other half

[Why before vs after the sublayer matters]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**LayerNorm** normalises each token's vector to zero mean, unit variance, then applies a learned scale and shift.

* Original transformer: LN *after* the sublayer ("Post-LN").
* Modern transformers: LN *before* ("Pre-LN", what we drew earlier).

The order matters for training stability — Pre-LN trains more reliably, especially at large scale.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.card}
**Why it works.** Activations across layers stay roughly the same scale, so gradients propagate through dozens of blocks. 

  * Combined with residuals, you get an architecture that's robust to depth.

Skipping LayerNorm in a 50-layer transformer turns it into a black hole of NaN loss.
:::
:::
:::

## Why each piece is there

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Multi-head attention**
: Lets every position look at every other (with causal mask).

**MLP** (a small feed-forward block)
: Position-wise non-linear processing. Standard 2-layer FNN with GELU activation.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**LayerNorm**
: Normalises activations per-token. Stabilises training of deep stacks.

**Residual connections**
: Each sublayer's output is **added** to its input. The identity path lets gradients flow through 100+ layers without vanishing (we saw the +1 trick two slides back).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Four pieces, four jobs: **attend** (look around), **process** (MLP), **normalise** (LayerNorm), **preserve the gradient** (residual). Keep this map — the Activity later asks you to match plain-English descriptions back to each one.
:::

## The full GPT architecture

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
* Token embedding **adds** positional embedding — attention is permutation-invariant otherwise.
* $N$ identical transformer blocks.
* Final LayerNorm, then a linear projection back to vocabulary size.
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-height: 5.0
digraph G {
  rankdir="TB"; bgcolor="transparent"; ranksep=0.34;
  // Graphviz sizes boxes with fallback metrics for Inter, which the browser
  // renders wider — the extra node margin keeps labels inside their shapes.
  node [fontname="Inter" fontsize=14 margin="0.30,0.14"];
  edge [fontname="Inter" fontsize=13];
  tok [shape=box label="Token embeddings\n(V × d)" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  pos [shape=box label="Positional embeddings\n(T × d)" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  add [shape=circle label="+" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  block1 [shape=box label="Transformer block 1" style=filled fillcolor="#C9322B" fontcolor="white"];
  blockN [shape=box label="Transformer block N" style=filled fillcolor="#C9322B" fontcolor="white"];
  ln [shape=box label="LayerNorm" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];
  head [shape=box label="Linear (d → V)" style=filled fillcolor="#1A6FB4" fontcolor="white"];
  out [shape=box label="next-token logits" style=filled fillcolor="#F4F1EA"];

  tok -> add; pos -> add;
  add -> block1 -> blockN [label="..." style=dashed];
  blockN -> ln -> head -> out;
}
```
:::
:::

## Counting GPT-2's parameters — the embeddings

We have counted the parameters of every architecture in this course, biases included. The transformer's turn.

::: {.card}
[GPT-2 small — the specification]{.eyebrow}

Vocabulary $V = 50{,}257$ · context $T = 1{,}024$ · width $d = 768$ · $N = 12$ blocks · $h = 12$ heads.
:::

::: {.card}
[The two embedding tables]{.eyebrow}

* **Token embeddings** — one $d$-vector per vocabulary entry: $50{,}257 \times 768 = 38{,}597{,}376$
* **Positional embeddings** — one $d$-vector per position: $1{,}024 \times 768 = 786{,}432$

Running total: $39{,}383{,}808$.
:::

[Lookup tables have no biases — nothing gets multiplied, so there is nothing to shift.]{.muted}

## Counting GPT-2's parameters — one block

Every linear layer costs (inputs × outputs) + outputs. Biases included, as always.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Attention]{.pill-blue}

* QKV projections, $d \to 3d$:
  $768 \times 2{,}304 + 2{,}304 = 1{,}771{,}776$
* Output projection $\mathbf{W}_O$, $d \to d$:
  $768 \times 768 + 768 = 590{,}592$
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[MLP]{.pill-blue}

* Up, $d \to 4d$:
  $768 \times 3{,}072 + 3{,}072 = 2{,}362{,}368$
* Down, $4d \to d$:
  $3{,}072 \times 768 + 768 = 2{,}360{,}064$
:::
:::

::: {.card}
Two LayerNorms, each a learned scale and shift per dimension: $2 \times 2 \times 768 = 3{,}072$.

One block: $1{,}771{,}776 + 590{,}592 + 2{,}362{,}368 + 2{,}360{,}064 + 3{,}072 = 7{,}087{,}872$.

Twelve blocks: $12 \times 7{,}087{,}872 = 85{,}054{,}464$.
:::

## Counting GPT-2's parameters — the total

::: {.card}
Two pieces left after the blocks:

* Final LayerNorm: $2 \times 768 = 1{,}536$.
* The $d \to V$ head **reuses the token embedding table**, transposed — this is **weight tying**. Cost: 0 new parameters.

$$
39{,}383{,}808 + 85{,}054{,}464 + 1{,}536 = 124{,}439{,}808 \approx 124\text{M}
$$

The famous number. When you read "GPT-2 small, 124M parameters", you can now account for every one of them.
:::

::: {.card}
[Where the parameters live]{.eyebrow}

| Component | Count | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Embeddings | $39{,}383{,}808$ | ~32% |
| MLPs | $56{,}669{,}184$ | ~46% |
| Attention | $28{,}348{,}416$ | ~23% |
| LayerNorms | $38{,}400$ | ~0.03% |

Attention gets the headlines; the MLPs hold nearly half the parameters.
:::

## What's the positional embedding doing?

[An aside that confuses students]{.eyebrow}

::: {.card}
Without positional information, attention is **permutation-invariant** — it would give the same output for `"dog bites man"` and `"man bites dog"`.

That's wrong. So we **add** a vector that encodes *which position* each token is in.

There are three common ways to build that position vector — **sinusoidal**, **learned**, and **RoPE** — which we compare next. The details matter for engineering, not for the core idea: *give every position a fingerprint the model can read.*
:::

## Positional encoding — three variants

[How to build the position fingerprint]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
[Sinusoidal]{.pill-blue}

Original transformer (2017). Deterministic, no learnable parameters. Embeds position $t$ as a vector of sines and cosines at different frequencies.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
[Learned]{.pill-blue}

One parameter vector per position, learned alongside the model. Used in BERT, GPT-2/3.

**Limitation**: can't extrapolate beyond training-time length.
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
[RoPE (rotary)]{.pill-green}

Rotates Q and K vectors by an angle proportional to position. Modern default — Llama, Mistral, Qwen.

Extrapolates more gracefully to longer contexts.
:::
:::

## Why attention is O(T²)

[The defining cost — and the limit it imposes]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
The attention matrix is $T \times T$.

For $T = 1{,}000$: 1M entries. Manageable.
For $T = 10{,}000$: 100M. Painful.
For $T = 1{,}000{,}000$: a *trillion* entries.

Compute cost scales as $T^2 \cdot d$ per layer. Memory scales as $T^2$.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.card}
**This is the dominant constraint** on context length.

* 1M-token GPT calls are possible but expensive.

Architectures like **Mamba**, **RingAttention**, and **Mixture-of-Depths** try reduce the $O(T^2)$ cost in different ways. 

Others like **FlashAttention** compute *exact* attention (so still $O(T^2)$ FLOPs) but use less memory.)

:::
:::
:::

## Training and inference — the contrast

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Training]{.pill-blue}

* Take a long sequence (say, 1024 tokens).
* Each position predicts the **next** token.
* Cross-entropy loss summed across all positions.
* All positions trained **in parallel** in one forward pass.

Recall, this parallelism is **why transformers won** over RNNs.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Inference]{.pill}

* Encode the prompt.
* Compute logits at the last position.
* Sample (or argmax) the next token.
* Append. Repeat.

**Auto-regressive**: one token at a time. The model never sees the next token before it predicts it.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Even though expensive, modern infrastructure can do this inferential step hundreds of times per second for tens of thousands of users simultaneously.
:::

## The KV cache — don't recompute what hasn't changed

The inference loop runs the model once per token. Most of that work is identical from step to step.

::: {.card}
When we generate token $T+1$, the keys and values of tokens $1 \ldots T$ **have not changed** — same tokens, same weights, same $\mathbf{k}_j$ and $\mathbf{v}_j$ as the last step.

The **KV cache**: keep every layer's keys and values in GPU memory. Each step then

1. computes one new query, key and value — for the new token only;
2. scores the new query against the cached keys;
3. appends the new key and value to the cache.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Without the cache]{.pill-amber}

Every new token recomputes attention for the whole prefix — all $T$ queries, keys and values, at every layer, every step.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[With the cache]{.pill-green}

Every new token computes one row of the attention matrix — one query against $T$ stored keys.
:::
:::

## The KV cache — worked example

The cache trades compute for memory. How much memory?

::: {.card}
[Per token cached — GPT-2 small, fp16]{.eyebrow}

$$
\underbrace{12}_{\text{layers}} \times \underbrace{2}_{K \text{ and } V} \times \underbrace{768}_{\text{width } d} \times \underbrace{2}_{\text{bytes (fp16)}} = 36{,}864 \text{ bytes} \approx 36 \text{ KB}
$$
:::

::: {.card}
[A 1,000-token conversation]{.eyebrow}

$$
1{,}000 \times 36{,}864 = 36{,}864{,}000 \text{ bytes} \approx 37 \text{ MB per sequence}
$$

Each "chat" carries its own cache. 

* GPT-2 small's weights in fp16 come to $124{,}439{,}808 \times 2 \approx 249$ MB

* Caches become the dominant source of GPU memory fill

:::

::: {.callout-note}
This is the $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ cost from earlier, paid at inference one row at a time: step $t$ does $\mathcal{O}(t)$ work against the cache, and $1 + 2 + \cdots + T$ still sums to $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$.
:::

# Part 3 · Scaling {background-color="#0E1A2B"}

## What changed as the models got bigger?

| Model | Params | Year | Train compute |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-1 | 117M | 2018 | tiny |
| GPT-2 | 1.5B | 2019 | ~1 GPU-month |
| GPT-3 | 175B | 2020 | ~3 GWh |
| GPT-4 | ~1.8T (estim.) | 2023 | tens of GWh |
| Claude 4.7 Opus | undisclosed | 2026 | undisclosed |

::: {.card}
The core block design is the same across these models. What changes:

* Width, depth, head count.
* Data: more tokens, better filtering.
* Training tricks: warmup, learning-rate schedules, fp16/bf16.
* **Post-training**: instruction tuning, RLHF — we don't cover this in detail.
:::

## Scaling laws

[Kaplan et al. (2020), Hoffmann et al. (2022)]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
Empirical regularity: model loss as a function of compute, parameters, and training tokens follows a **power law**.

* Doubling parameters → ~constant fractional drop in loss.
* Same for doubling data, or doubling compute.
* Extends over many orders of magnitude.

**Chinchilla** (2022): the "optimal" allocation is roughly **20 tokens per parameter** — the previous era over-parameterised and under-trained.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.card}
The reason every lab now trains for as long as they can afford. The reason "more data + more compute" is the answer to most questions.

The reason **the cost of being at the frontier doubles every ~6 months** — and the reason there are now only ~5 organisations on the frontier.
:::
:::
:::

## Your turn — Chinchilla maths

[<span class="pause-cue">≈ 3 min</span>]{.eyebrow}

::: {.try-box}
[Try]{.try-label}
You're training a **1-billion-parameter** model. Chinchilla says compute-optimal is **~20 tokens per parameter**.

1. How many training tokens should you aim for?

2. Your budget only stretches to **5 billion** tokens. Over- or under-parameterised — and what would you change, the model or the data?
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.reveal-box}
[Answer]{.reveal-label}
1. $20 \times 1{,}000{,}000{,}000 = 20$ **billion tokens**.
2. With only 5B tokens you'd feed a 1B model a quarter of its optimal data — **under-trained / over-parameterised**. The Chinchilla fix: **shrink the model** to ~250M params ($5\text{B} \div 20$) so it matches the data, *or* go find 15B more tokens.
:::
:::

## "Emergent" capabilities

A surprise of the GPT-3 era:

> Capabilities like multi-step arithmetic, code synthesis, and translation **don't gradually improve** with scale — they appear roughly *step-wise* once a model gets big enough.

::: {.callout-warning}
# This is an **active debate** 

Is "emergence" real or a measurement artefact (Schaeffer et al. 2023). Either way, the practical consequence is the same: **scale unlocks capabilities you didn't know to test for**.

For policy and ethics, this matters: the model that ships next year may have abilities the model in your lab doesn't.
:::

## Mixture of experts — the inference trick

[A way to grow parameter count without growing inference cost]{.eyebrow}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**The idea**: replace the dense feed-forward sublayer with a *bank* of feed-forward "experts". A small router network picks ~2 of them per token.

* Total params: huge (8× or 16× a dense model).
* Active params *per token*: only the picked experts.
* Inference cost: stays low.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.card}
Used by:

* **Mixtral 8×7B** (Mistral, 2023).
* **GPT-4** (rumoured to be MoE).
* **DeepSeek V3** and Gemini.

The 2024+ frontier is increasingly MoE. The same architecture-stacking principle — but with sparsity along the depth axis.
:::
:::
:::

## Limitations even at scale

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Computational]{.pill-amber}

* The $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ attention cost (Part 2) still caps practical context length.
* Generation is **sequential** — one token at a time, so latency grows with output length.
* Inference cost is real — every API call burns energy.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Conceptual]{.pill-amber}

* Hallucination is **built into the architecture**.
* No internal "truth" signal.
* Brittle reasoning under distribution shift.
* Encodes biases of training data.

We come back to ethics on Day 12.
:::
:::

## A connection to social science — LLMs as instruments

::: {.card}
A live research question: can LLMs be used as **measurement instruments** for social-scientific constructs?

* Argyle et al. (2023): can an LLM "simulate" a respondent of a given demographic? (Partially, with caveats.)
* Spirling (2023): argues social science should rely on **open** models, not closed APIs, so that text-based measurements stay reproducible. (A live methodological debate.)
* @bender2021stochastic — *Stochastic Parrots* — raises the deeper question of whether asking these models for **meaning** at all is a category error.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
These debates are about **the exact architecture you'll have built by today's lab**. You're now equipped to read them critically.
:::

[<span class="pause-cue">Where you are at the end of Day 10</span>]{.eyebrow}

::: {.card}
You can:

1. State, in one sentence, what attention does.
2. Take a sequence of embeddings all the way to an attention output by hand.
3. Say why a model runs several heads, and how the width $d$ is split between them.
4. Name every component of a transformer block.
5. Explain why residuals + LayerNorm enable deep stacks.
6. Describe the difference between training (parallel) and inference (autoregressive).
7. Articulate at least one debate over what LLMs *mean* for social science.

**This is the architecture behind GPT, Claude, and every modern LLM.**

:::
